blocks.text: On Monday, 5 people in Riverton got sick. By Friday, the health department knew about only 2 of them. What happened to the others?

chunks.text: Germs that cause outbreaks travel in a **chain of infection**: a germ lives in a **reservoir**, leaves the body, travels through a **vehicle** such as food or water, enters a new person, and finds a **susceptible host**. Break any link and the chain stops.

Health departments watch for outbreaks using **surveillance**: ongoing collection of illness data. But surveillance sees only the **tip of the iceberg**. Many people stay home or are never tested, and reports arrive days late.

steps.caption: Imagine 1,000 people become ill from one outbreak.
Only some of those are tested at a lab.
Only some test results are reported, and days later. The department sees about 50 of 1,000.

blocks.title: Worked example: where is the chain broken?
steps: Situation: A pool is contaminated and 30 swimmers get sick.
Reservoir: a sick swimmer. Vehicle: the pool water. Host: other swimmers.
Where can we break the chain? Close the pool (stop the vehicle) or disinfect the water.
Notice that treating each sick swimmer does not stop new people from getting sick.

bullets: The chain of infection has six links; break any one to stop spread.
The vehicle carries the germ from the reservoir to new hosts.
Surveillance sees only part of the illness: the tip of the pyramid.
Reports lag behind illness, so the newest days look low.
